body:
A commercial property buying brief should record your intended use, preferred locations, practical site requirements, budget inputs, timing and decision process. For a Newcastle business buying its own premises, the first question is whether a property can support the business you intend to operate. Price and floor area matter, but they do not answer that question by themselves.

This guide helps Newcastle and Hunter owner-occupiers prepare for a commercial buyers agent meeting. It provides inspection and briefing prompts, without investment forecasts, promised savings or claims about completed projects.

## Define the business use before the search

Explain what happens at the premises on a normal day: people arriving, equipment operating, stock moving, visitors attending and deliveries being made. Describe any planned changes. A business expecting more staff or different equipment may need a different property from one continuing its current operations.

Record the requirements that would rule a site out, and distinguish them from features that would be convenient. Your appointed planning and technical advisers assess whether a particular property can accommodate the proposed use and any required changes.

## Write the practical requirements in a comparison sheet

Use the same questions for every property. A consistent brief helps prevent a well-presented listing from distracting you from access, usable space or operational constraints.

| Requirement | Record before inspections | Check for each property |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proposed use | Current activities and expected changes | What specialist checks are needed for this use? |
| Usable space | Work areas, meeting needs, equipment and storage | Can the required layout fit the actual floor plan? |
| Access | Staff, visitor, delivery and vehicle requirements | Are access arrangements suitable and documented? |
| Location | Newcastle or Hunter search area and travel priorities | Does the site work for staff, customers and suppliers? |
| Existing condition | Items that could be retained and changes required | What needs investigation, pricing or specialist review? |
| Timing | Target occupation and current lease constraints | Can settlement, approvals, works and moving be coordinated? |

These prompts are not a building inspection or an approval checklist. They help identify which evidence to request and which specialists need to be involved.

## Agree the search area with reasons

A Newcastle CBD office, a Maryville premises and a property elsewhere in Lake Macquarie or the Hunter may serve different operational needs. Specify the acceptable travel patterns, customer access and delivery requirements instead of assuming one suburb is always the best option.

Include alternatives you would genuinely consider. Keep the reason for each location preference visible so the search can expand sensibly if suitable premises are limited.

## Keep acquisition and occupation budgets separate

Work with your appointed finance, accounting and legal advisers to define the purchase parameters and required allowances. Record transaction costs, professional fees, fit out, furniture, moving and potential holding costs separately from the advertised property price.

If a figure has not been confirmed, label it as an allowance to verify. YOS coordinates the commercial property workstream; it does not provide legal, tax, financial, credit or investment advice. A commercial property buying brief does not establish borrowing capacity or suitability for an SMSF.

## Plan inspections around evidence

Before an inspection, identify the questions the listing leaves unanswered. Request available plans and relevant property information through the appropriate channels. During the visit, record what you observed separately from what an agent stated and what still needs checking.

For example, visible space for equipment does not confirm that the building services can support it. An accessible driveway does not establish that every required delivery vehicle can use it. Follow up material assumptions with the appropriate adviser rather than treating an inspection impression as proof.

## Confirm responsibilities before engaging a buyers agent

Ask for a clear scope covering the search, opportunity assessment, negotiation and coordination tasks. Discuss fees, authority and how potential conflicts or relevant payment arrangements are handled before work begins. NSW Government guidance explains written agency agreements for property professionals; your engagement should be reviewed for the services actually being appointed.

[Read NSW Government guidance on agency agreements](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/agency-agreements)

## Frequently asked questions

### When should I speak with a commercial buyers agent?

Ideally before narrowing the search to one property. The brief can connect the business requirements, search criteria and decision process before inspection or negotiation pressure builds.

### Can I prepare a brief before finance is finalised?

Yes. You can document operational needs and working assumptions while your finance advisers assess the funding pathway. Do not present unconfirmed purchase capacity as approved finance.

### Is this the same as residential buyers agency?

No. This guide concerns commercial premises and the business activities they must support. YOS's service scope is commercial property buying in NSW.

### Does a buyers agent undertake all due diligence?

No. Your appointed solicitor, accountant, valuer, building consultant and other specialists advise in their own areas. YOS coordinates the agreed commercial property workstream and their inputs into the decision.

### Can YOS help with the workplace after purchase?

Yes. Client-side office fit out project management and commercial furniture support can be considered under separately agreed scopes, based on the property's requirements and your programme.
